rv.q: Rupert Goold’s production is still a magnificent piece of theatrical craft that fuses sport and art.
I’m delighted to report that Dear England, populist and profound simultaneously, remains a towering achievement.
This remains a brilliant, state-of-the-nation piece: a wise, big-hearted, pulsating drama that explores, with Shakespearean wit and sweep, huge issues.
Even so, the inclusive fascination and adrenal fervour of the evening remains.
That it remains powerful and poignant theatre is a sign of how convincingly the play speaks to profound themes beyond results on the pitch.
A weakness remains the simplicity of some minor characters.
The three-hour show feels a bit flabby.
It is a winning performance in a play that is vital in every way – both full of life, and of essential debate.

Between hope, failure, community and blasts of "Sweet Caroline", Dear England is a show that will have British audiences dancing in the stands with celebration of a nation that, while often wrong-footing itself, is steadfast in its love of the game.
Directed by Rupert Goold, is a powerful and punchy production that captures the heart of the nation's sport.
That aside, Dear England is undoubtedly thoughtful, detailed, entertaining and absorbing.
The penalty kick becomes the totem of both Southgate’s approach and the play itself
It’s still a blast, and worth reflecting on what it is about James Graham’s work that, on any topic, stirs the heart.

cn.t: James Graham's Olivier-winning play about Gareth Southgate's England tenure scores again with critics, who praise its emotional resonance, crowd-pleasing energy, and brilliant exploration of national identity through football.
